At a collision \(\theta_i=\theta_j\) the symmetric coupled shifts
are equal, so \(y_i-y_j\) vanishes to first order. The raw numerator
is bounded by \(C^{N^2}\rho^{N(N-1)}\), including its regular pair
denominators. After \(j\) Lie jets and one conservative flux/cutoff
loss, its remaining coarea power is
\(L=N^2-2j-4\ge4N_0+1>0\).
The exact inequalities \(d\le2\rho\) and \(\rho\le\sqrt N\,d\)
show that the near region
has \(\rho\le\sqrt N\,N^{-K_0}\), not literally \(\rho\le N^{-K_0}\).
Taking fixed \(K_0>1\) and increasing it if needed gives
\[
 C^{N^2}(\sqrt N\,N^{-K_0})^L
      e^{O_j(N\log(N+1))}(H+\log N)^2
 \le e^{C_jN\log(N+1)}(H+N)^{C_j}.
\]
The simple phase kernels have attenuation floors \(cN\eps\) in
this window. On each fixed shape ray, \(F=N\mu\) and bounded individual
phases put the unwrapped image inside a rectangle with side lengths
at most \(CN\). The multiplicity-one statement above, followed by
the interval estimate in Appendix~\ref{app:lie}, bounds its phase
integral by \(CN^2(H+\log N)^2\). This explicit polynomial factor
is included in \(e^{O_j(N\log(N+1))}\) in the displayed estimate.

\section{The onsite series and the infinite odd-particle tail}\label{sec:conclusion}

\begin{proposition}[The onsite differentiated series]\label{prop:onsitesum}
At either selected boundary half, for every fixed nonnegative integer
$j$, there are constants such that, with $H=\log(1/\eps)$,
\[
 \sum_{\substack{N\ge1\\N\ {\rm odd}}}|f_N^{(j)}(t_\eps)|
 \le C_j\exp\bigl(B_j\log^2(H+1)\bigr).
\]
In particular this sum is $o(\eps^{-\delta})$ for every $\delta>0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First work in the positive-$S_*$ geometry. The reduced onsite form
has global factor $(YZ)^{-1}$ and the same complete pairs and
one-body measures. The same homotopy and weighted Cartan identity
give $f_N=F_{00,N}+K_{00,N}+S_{00,N}$, with precisely the same
current multiplier $-2\ii\tau\,\partial_q\psi$. There are no
global product poles. The proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:F} applies
with these denominators deleted, and its all-$N$ summable majorant
therefore bounds $\sum|F_{00,N}^{(j)}|$ by the displayed subpower
function of $\eps^{-1}$.

\section{The onsite series and the infinite odd-particle tail}\label{sec:conclusion}

separately before the tail is assembled. Its contour has no global
product poles, so a one-phase regularization suffices. The final theorem
then combines the onsite bound with the four offsite estimates from

\begin{remark}[Independent physical check of the onsite sum]
The classical per-site identity in \cite[eqs.~(4.1)--(4.2)]{Orrick2001}
also gives an independent check of the full-site normalization.
At the origin its angular integrand has no displacement multiplier:
by Lemma~\ref{lem:residue} it is precisely $f_N$.
Since $\langle\sigma_{00}^2\rangle=1$, for real $t>1$ it follows that
\[
 t(1-t^{-4})^{1/4}\sum_{N\ {\rm odd}}f_N(t)=1.
\]
Local normal convergence and the identity theorem extend this equality
throughout $|t|>1$, with the fourth root inherited from infinity.
Consequently
\[
 \mathcal X_H(1/t)=1+2t(1-t^{-4})^{1/4}
                    \sum_{N\ {\rm odd}}T_N(t).
\]
This supplies a second final bridge using only the offsite tail.
The preceding proposition proves the stronger absolute onsite
derivative bound directly and also permits the full-coefficient
tail statement below. No identity involving a generalized
correlation function or a Painlev\'e extension is used here.
\end{remark}

\section{Noncancellation and the natural boundary}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
Put $U(t)=\sum_{N\ge1,\,N\ {\rm odd}}C_N(t)$. For each selected
point, the finitely many lower terms have bounded derivatives.
Theorems~\ref{thm:first} and \ref{thm:tail} give
\[
 U^{(k)}(t_\eps)=4L_*\eps^{-1}+o(\eps^{-1}),
 \qquad U^{(j)}(t_\eps)=o(\eps^{-1})\quad(0\le j<k).
\]
Define $\widehat{\mathcal X}(t)=\mathcal X_H(1/t)$.
By \eqref{eq:bulk},
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal X}(t)=Q_H(t)U(t),\qquad
 Q_H(t)=t(1-t^{-4})^{1/4}.
\]
At our selected nonaxis points $Q_H$ is locally analytic and
nonzero on its chosen continuation. Leibniz's rule therefore gives
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal X}^{(k)}(t_\eps)
 =4Q_H(t_*)L_*\eps^{-1}+o(\eps^{-1}),
 \qquad Q_H(t_*)L_*\ne0.
\]
A holomorphic continuation through $t_*$ would bound this finite
derivative on a short exterior radial segment, a contradiction.
The selected points are dense in both upper quadrants, and
conjugation supplies both lower quadrants. Every neighborhood of
every point of $|t|=1$, including an axis point, contains one of
these obstructing points. Thus no point of the circle permits
local holomorphic continuation of the exterior germ.

\section{Fixed-cutoff differentiation, pole counting, and coarea}
\label{app:lie}

This appendix provides the calculus used in the intermediate-order
sectors. The order of operations is fixed: differentiate on a smooth,
fixed real domain; verify that the puncture fluxes vanish; then estimate
the resulting absolute integral by coarea. Freezing the two product
phases keeps their kernels simple during differentiation.

the cutoffs are smooth on the closed torus. These flux checks
apply at every earlier stage \(0\le l\le j\), and establish the
iterated identity before any boundary-uniform estimate is taken.

\paragraph{Coupled occupancy and changed pairs .}
The compact-right current field may move a coordinate where
\(p'\ne0\). The exact contour Jacobian gives
\[
 (V\cdot\nabla\log y_i)_{\rm occ}
   =\frac{\lambda\tau}{2N}m_i\sum_l V_l p'_l.
\]
An individual off-diagonal entry is \(O(\lambda\tau/N)\).
The compact-right field has two nonzero components, each possibly
\(O(N/|\theta_p-\theta_q|)\), so the contraction can be
\(O(\lambda\tau/|\theta_p-\theta_q|)\). It moves every
\(m\)-supported root and must be retained. All these roots are
compact in this chart; no singular raw branch-angle jet is used.

\paragraph{Background and physical input.}
The fixed-particle singularities and their accumulation on the unit
circle motivate the natural-boundary question for the complete
susceptibility. Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann, and Perk
\cite[Section~3.2]{Orrick2001} studied their amplitudes and the possible
survival of these singularities in the infinite sum. Boukraa et al.
\cite{Boukraa2008} developed further series and singularity evidence.
The issue addressed here is uniform control of the complete
differentiated tail, which turns a first-particle singularity into an
obstruction for the bulk sum.

source_context.text:
\paragraph{Provenance and mathematical inputs.}
The physical form-factor identity below is the classical full bulk
identity, in the precise normalization of \cite[eqs.~(1.9), (1.11),
(3.13), (3.17)--(3.20)]{Orrick2001} and \cite[eqs.~(3), (5)--(9)]{Boukraa2008}.
The contour partition and tail estimates adapt the method of manuscript
v0.1-rc6, at commit
\texttt{2cf997226db314ad52fa40a2ecda5439542606bf} \cite{Snapshot};
the adapted arguments are proved here. The physical identity is the
external statistical-mechanical input. The remaining argument derives
the analytic obstruction from the odd-particle integrals. In particular,
the fixed-order gradient method of \cite{TW2014} is established at the
selected odd orders, including the additional negative-real-part endpoint

\paragraph{Background and physical input.}
The fixed-particle singularities and their accumulation on the unit
circle motivate the natural-boundary question for the complete
susceptibility. Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann, and Perk
\cite[Section~3.2]{Orrick2001} studied their amplitudes and the possible
survival of these singularities in the infinite sum. Boukraa et al.
\cite{Boukraa2008} developed further series and singularity evidence.

differentiated tail, which turns a first-particle singularity into an
obstruction for the bulk sum.

The physical form-factor identity below is the classical full bulk
identity, in the precise normalization of \cite[eqs.~(1.9), (1.11),
(3.13), (3.17)--(3.20)]{Orrick2001} and \cite[eqs.~(3), (5)--(9)]{Boukraa2008}.
The contour partition and tail estimates apply to the full
odd-particle series. The physical identity is the external
statistical-mechanical input; the analytic estimates for the
odd-particle integrals are proved in the following sections. We also adapt the gradient argument of Tracy and Widom
\cite{TW2014} to the selected odd orders, treating the additional
negative-real-part endpoint case explicitly.

source_context.text:
\paragraph{How to read the proof.}
The geometric picture is a boundary point at which the first admissible
particle contribution becomes singular, while the full remaining series
stays smaller after the same finite number of derivatives. Sections
\ref{sec:setup}--\ref{sec:first} identify the complete lattice observable,
select these points, and calculate the first singularity. Section
\ref{sec:signs} reduces both boundary halves to one signed family.
Sections \ref{sec:tailreduction}--\ref{sec:sectors} supply the uniform
estimates needed for the infinite sum; Section \ref{sec:conclusion}
assembles them, and Section 11 completes the noncancellation argument.
Appendix \ref{app:lie} gives the differentiation and coarea calculus used
in the sector estimates. Appendix \ref{app:constants} records the order
in which all constants are fixed.

semicircle and their imaginary-part ratios agree. Along

\[

left in \cite[footnote~5]{TW2014}; no even-order theorem is being
applied to it. With neither product vector, a nonzero dispersion
vector cannot cancel, since $S_*\notin\{-2,0,2\}$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textbf{4. Evaluate the coefficient and add the charts.} Let $\mathscr C_p=p^{-1/2}\int_{\sum\omega_i=0,\,|\omega|=1}
\Delta(\omega)^2\dd\sigma(\omega)>0$. Polar coordinates give
\[
 \int_{\R^{p-1}}\frac{\Delta(u)^2\dd u}
 {(Q-\ii d\sum u_i^2)^{k+1}}
 =\frac{\mathscr C_p}{2}Q^{-1}(-\ii d)^{-k}B(k,1)
 =\frac{\mathscr C_p}{2kQd^k}.
\]
For an elementary evaluation set $c=-\ii d$ and $x=|u|^2$ in
the radial integral. The exact identity
\[
 \frac{\dd}{\dd x}\left(\frac{cx}{Q+cx}\right)^k
 =kQc^k\frac{x^{k-1}}{(Q+cx)^{k+1}}
\]
has endpoint values zero and one, and $Q+cx\ne0$ for $x\ge0$.
It proves the displayed integral without any continuation of
a noninteger power. Since $k\equiv0\pmod4$,
$d^k=|d|^k>0$ for either sign of $S_*$. The ordinary Gaussian
Vandermonde integral is
\[
 \int_{\R^p}e^{-|x|^2/2}\Delta(x)^2\dd x
 =(2\pi)^{p/2}\prod_{m=1}^p m!.
\]
For completeness, expand the two Vandermonde determinants in monic
Hermite polynomials. Orthogonality gives $p!$ times the product of
their squared norms $\sqrt{2\pi}\,m!$, $0\le m<p$, obtained by
integration by parts from the Rodrigues formula. Separate the unit
mean coordinate and polar coordinates on its orthogonal complement
to obtain
\[
 \mathscr C_p=
 \frac{(2\pi)^{(p-1)/2}\prod_{m=1}^p m!}
 {\sqrt p\,2^{k-1}(k-1)!}.
\]
Substitution cancels every power of $\sin\beta$ and yields exactly
$L_*$ in \eqref{eq:amplitudeclosed}. Exchanging $\alpha,\beta$
leaves this expression unchanged, so the two ordered charts add.
The fixed onsite coefficient is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:complement},
and \eqref{eq:onsiteidentity} gives the factor four for $C_p$.
Equivalently the full angular representation has four equal charts
at $\pm\alpha,\pm\beta$. Finally the same radial bound at derivative
order $k-1$ is logarithmic, and through order $k-2$ is integrable
at $\eps=0$. The displaced sides and complement are already bounded.
\end{proof}

Here is the uniform mixed-pair calculation. On the entire protected
disk a true branch root \(w\) remains in the closed lower unit disk:
its \(W\)-image has strictly positive imaginary part by the
\(P/N\) margin. The compact radial-center root \(z_0\) belongs to
a fixed compact subset of that same half-disk excluding \(\pm1\).
Thus for some \(g>0\), either \(|z_0|\le1-g\) or
\(\Im z_0\le-g\). In both cases \(|1-z_0w|\ge g\).
For the second case this follows directly from
\[
 |z_0|^2|1-z_0w|^2
 =(|z_0|^2\Re w-\Re z_0)^2+
   (|z_0|^2\Im w+\Im z_0)^2.
\]
The compact root moves to \(z\) by at most \(L/N\); reduce the
disk constant so this is at most \(g/2\). With
\(A(z,w)=(z-w)/(1-zw)\),
\[
 A(z,w)-A(z_0,w)=\frac{(z-z_0)(1-w^2)}{(1-zw)(1-z_0w)},\qquad
 |A(z,w)|\le1+\frac{4L}{g^2N}.
\]
Only the compact root was displaced in this comparison: \(w\)
is held at its actual disk-point value. Hence no square-root branch
motion enters the estimate. Compact roots on both transition supports
are covered by the two compact groups, and no perturbed compact root
is assumed to lie in the unit disk. For compatibility with the existing
budget we may weaken this bound to \(1+C/\sqrt N\) in the next display.
Since the same-group count is at least \(M^2/4-M/2\),
\[
 |\Pf\widehat A(z)|\le
 \exp(CN+CM\sqrt N-aM^2)\le C_1^N e^{-a_1M^2}.
\]
The last inequality uses
\(CM\sqrt N\le(a/2)M^2+C^2N/(2a)\); the mixed inflation cannot be
dropped without this step.

\begin{remark}[Independent physical check of the onsite sum]
The classical per-site identity in \cite[eqs.~(4.1)--(4.2)]{Orrick2001}
also gives an independent check of the full-site normalization.
At the origin its angular integrand has no displacement multiplier:
by Lemma~\ref{lem:residue} it is precisely $f_N$.
Since $\langle\sigma_{00}^2\rangle=1$, for real $t>1$ it follows that
\[
 t(1-t^{-4})^{1/4}\sum_{N\ {\rm odd}}f_N(t)=1.
\]
Local normal convergence and the identity theorem extend this equality
throughout $|t|>1$, with the fourth root inherited from infinity.
Consequently
\[
 \mathcal X_H(1/t)=1+2t(1-t^{-4})^{1/4}
                    \sum_{N\ {\rm odd}}T_N(t).
\]
This supplies a second final bridge using only the offsite tail.
The preceding proposition proves the stronger absolute onsite
derivative bound directly and also permits the full-coefficient
tail statement below. The check uses the physical per-site identity and the identity theorem
on the exterior domain.
\end{remark}

The high-temperature susceptibility of the square-lattice Ising model
is represented by an infinite series of odd-particle integrals. The
singularities of individual terms accumulate densely on the unit circle,
and their survival in the complete sum is the central analytic issue.
Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann, and Perk \cite[Section~3.2]{Orrick} and
Boukraa et al.\ \cite{Boukraa} studied the singularities and the series
evidence for a natural boundary. We use a balanced deformation of the constrained angular integral,
a regular inverse coordinate, and a single tangential field to
estimate the full differentiated tail.

\section{The physical function and the proof}
Let $J>0$ and consider the zero-field isotropic Ising model on the
infinite square lattice. For $0<s=\sinh(2\beta_{\rm phys}J)<1$,
let
\[
 \X(s)=\beta_{\rm phys}^{-1}\chi_H(s)
       =\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2}\langle\sigma_{00}\sigma_{mn}\rangle_s.
\]
The high-temperature infinite-volume Gibbs state has zero
magnetization. This sum includes every lattice site and its origin.

\section{The physical function and the proof}
The high-temperature susceptibility of the square-lattice Ising model
is represented by an infinite series of odd-particle integrals. The
singularities of individual terms accumulate densely on the unit circle,
and their survival in the complete sum is the central analytic issue.
Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann, and Perk \cite[Section~3.2]{Orrick} and
Boukraa et al.\ \cite{Boukraa} studied the singularities and the series
evidence for a natural boundary. We use a balanced deformation of the constrained angular integral,
a regular inverse coordinate, and a single tangential field to
estimate the full differentiated tail.

Let $J>0$ and consider the zero-field isotropic Ising model on the
infinite square lattice. For $0<s=\sinh(2\beta_{\rm phys}J)<1$,
let
\[
 \X(s)=\beta_{\rm phys}^{-1}\chi_H(s)
       =\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2}\langle\sigma_{00}\sigma_{mn}\rangle_s.
\]
The high-temperature infinite-volume Gibbs state has zero
magnetization. This sum includes every lattice site and its origin.
We use $t=s^{-1}$ only as an exterior coordinate and put
\[
 S(t)=t+t^{-1},\qquad Q_H(t)=t(1-t^{-4})^{1/4},
\]
where the fourth root tends to one at infinity.

The bordered determinant identity proved in
Section~\ref{sec:elementary-pfaffian} has size $N+1$ with bounded
entries on a common small complex angular strip. There the
one-body factors are bounded and $|z_i|\le e^{-c}<1$.
Shifting every angle by $\ii\eta\operatorname{sgn}(n)$, for
fixed sufficiently small $\eta>0$, gives
\[
 |c_N(m,n;t)|\le \frac{C^N N^{(N+1)/2}}{N!}
                   e^{-N(c|m|+\eta|n|)}.
\]
Periodicity justifies the shift; Hadamard supplies the determinant
bound. This is summable in $m,n$ and all odd $N$.
Thus particle and lattice sums may be interchanged.
The $m$-sum gives $(1+Z)/(1-Z)$.
For a periodic analytic $F$ on $\T^N$, define
\[
 A(v)=\int_{\T^{N-1}}
 F(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{N-1},v-\textstyle\sum_{i<N}\theta_i)
                   \prod_{i<N}\frac{\dd\theta_i}{2\pi}.
\]
Its Fourier coefficient of index $-n$ is the $N$-angle integral
with multiplier $e^{\ii n\sum\theta_i}$.
The absolutely convergent Fourier sum is $A(0)$, giving precisely
\eqref{eq:angular-bulk}, with no lost $2\pi$ factor.
At the origin the per-site sum is $\langle\sigma_{00}^2\rangle=1$,
so the origin is already contained in this full-lattice sum.
For a further normalization check,
\[
 C_1(t)=\frac1{S(t)-2}=\frac{s}{(1-s)^2}.
\]

For every fixed finite positive coupling ratio, we establish natural
boundaries for the complete bulk magnetic susceptibility on both
physical temperature sides. The high-temperature domain is a bounded
lens; the low-temperature domain is a simply connected epigraph.
We first determine these domains from an independently defined spectral
set and then prove that their full boundaries obstruct continuation.
At regular positive edges, and at either sign of a low-temperature edge,
a nonzero first singular amplitude dominates the entire differentiated
particle tail. Negative high-temperature edges require a different
mechanism: the odd-particle constraint excludes an exact endpoint
resonance, so we use an exact symmetric pole normal form, a
dimension-uniform beta-period estimate, and dominance of one particle
index in selected high Taylor coefficients. The isotropic case follows
from an exact coefficient match to the normalized isotropic results.
The proof retains every lattice site, all particle orders, the physical
field normalization, and the pure-phase low-temperature magnetization
subtraction. Its inputs are the cited real-temperature spin form factors
and the explicitly identified isotropic analytic theorems.
\end{abstract}
\section*{Introduction}
The form-factor expansion expresses the magnetic susceptibility of the
square-lattice Ising model as an infinite sum of multiple integrals.
The singularities of the individual integrals and their possible
cancellation in the complete sum are central to its complex-temperature
analyticity. Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann and Perk \cite[Section 3.2]{ONGP}
studied the order dependence of the isotropic singularity amplitudes.
Boukraa, Hassani and Maillard \cite[Section 6.2]{BHM} described the
anisotropic cosine-grid singularity equations in two complex couplings
and their accumulation. Restricting the physical coupling ratio fixes
a one-variable temperature problem, whose spectral geometry and
complete-sum obstruction are the subjects of this paper.

We prove the natural-boundary theorem on the explicit high-temperature
lens and low-temperature epigraph stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:aniso}.
The published spin form factors of Bugrij and Lisovyy \cite{BL} and
Iorgov and Lisovyy \cite{IL} identify the physical coefficients.
The regular-edge proof separates a nonzero first singular derivative
from the entire differentiated tail. At negative high-temperature
edges, the obstruction instead comes from the growth of boundary
Taylor coefficients. The equal-coupling case follows from the
isotropic natural-boundary theorems of Lin \cite{LTsource,HTsource}
through the exact coefficient identities in Section~\ref{sec:closure}.

\subsection{Field normalization and state}
Let the magnetic field have energy units, so the finite-volume Hamiltonian
contains $-h\sum_v\sigma_v$, with $\sigma_v\in\{-1,1\}$ and magnetic
moment set to one. Direct differentiation of the finite partition
function gives
\[
 \left.\frac{\partial\langle\sigma_0\rangle}{\partial h}\right|_{h=0}
 =\beta\sum_v\bigl(\langle\sigma_0\sigma_v\rangle
                         -\langle\sigma_0\rangle\langle\sigma_v\rangle\bigr).
\]
Thus the normalized response is the covariance sum $\mathcal X$, and
$\chi=\beta\mathcal X$. A dimensionless field $\eta=\beta h$ instead
has response $\mathcal X$. A specified nonunit magnetic moment multiplies
both by its square.

source_context.text:
The covariance sum also equals the literal uniform-field derivative after
the thermodynamic limit. Here is a precise justification once its finite
absolute sum, proved below, is available. The GHS inequality for arbitrary
nonnegative couplings and site fields \cite[Theorem 1.5]{CGN} says that
truncated two-spin correlations decrease as any nonnegative site field
increases. Pinning the spins removed from a larger plus box by fields
tending to $+\infty$ consequently shows that the plus-box covariances
increase with the box. Their sums converge monotonically to $\mathcal X$.
If $m_V(h)=\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{V,+,h}$, GHS also makes $m_V$
concave for $h\ge0$. Thus
\[
 m_V(h)-m_V(0)\le h m'_V(0)
 =\beta h\sum_{v\in V}\operatorname{Cov}_{V,+,0}(\sigma_0,\sigma_v)
 \le\beta h\mathcal X.
\]
Passing to the plus-state limit gives the upper right-derivative bound
$m'(0+)\le\beta\mathcal X$. Conversely, turn on $h$ only in a finite
set $E$ in the infinite plus state. This is a bounded local change of
measure, so its derivative at zero is exactly
$\beta\sum_{v\in E}\operatorname{Cov}_{+,0}(\sigma_0,\sigma_v)$.
Ferromagnetic field monotonicity makes the uniform-field magnetization
at least this local-field magnetization, with equality at $h=0$.
Letting $E$ increase to the lattice gives the reverse derivative bound.
Hence $m'(0+)=\beta\mathcal X$. In HT, spin-flip symmetry gives the
same derivative from the other side; in LT the stated one-sided
pure-phase convention applies. This argument does not exchange an
uncontrolled magnetic-field limit with an infinite sum.

The exact full-site multiplier in the double contour is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allsites}
 \frac{(1+X)(1+Y)}{XY(1-X)(1-Y)}
 =\frac1{XY}+\frac{2(X^{-1}+Y^{-1})}{(1-X)(1-Y)}.
\end{equation}
It is the product of the two sums $\sum_{m\in\Z}X^{|m|-1}$ and
$\sum_{l\in\Z}Y^{|l|-1}$. It counts the origin once, each reflected
axis correctly, and all four open quadrants. If $C_N$ is the full-site
coefficient and $T_N$ the contour with the second numerator but without
its factor two, then $C_N=f_N(0,0)+2T_N$. The onsite sums are one in
the HT phase and $1-M^2$ after the LT subtraction. No axis or onsite
contribution is discarded.

\section{Regular spectral edges: whole amplitudes and the entire tail}
\label{sec:regular}

At a regular boundary point exactly one of the two real spectral
coordinates is $+1$ or $-1$, the other lies strictly between them, and
the corresponding edge map is a nonramified holomorphic local
coordinate. Interchange the transfer axes when necessary. First take
the endpoint $q_0=0$ and write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positiveedge}
 W(q;u)=b+u+B(u)(1-\cos q),\qquad
 b=\cos\phi,\quad 0<\phi<\pi,\quad \Im B(0)>0.
\end{equation}
Here $u=W(0)-b$ vanishes at the selected point. The opposite sign of
$\Im B$ is obtained by complex conjugation. On the edge, $W(q)$ is
in the upper half-plane except at $q=0$. Its canonical root
$\rho(q)=e^{-\gamma(q)}$ lies in the lower half-disk, with
$\rho(0)=e^{-\ii\phi}$. Compactness gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:halfdisc}
 \Im\rho(q)\le-\delta<0,\qquad |\rho(q)|\le1
 \quad(q\in\R).
\end{equation}
There is no real-angle point with $W=\pm1$. The root, a local
$\gamma$, and all one-body and canceled-pair denominators are therefore
holomorphic on a common fixed complex parameter and angular
neighborhood. On the physical-domain approach $u=\ii\eps$, $\eps>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:attenuation}
 \Re\gamma(q;\ii\eps)\ge c\bigl(\eps+\dist(q,0)^2\bigr).
\end{equation}
Indeed $\Im W=\eps+\Im B(\ii\eps)(1-\cos q)$ is bounded below by
that expression, while
$\Im W=\sinh(\Re\gamma)\sin(\Im\gamma)$ on the compact chosen branch.
The same local side belongs to the physical component bordering the
regular edge, by the geometry of Section~\ref{sec:geometry}.

The elementary identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:schurdifference}

and \eqref{eq:halfdisc} give a constant $\rho_0<1$ such that

fixed complex parameter neighborhood. This assertion continues to hold

\begin{lemma}[Matched-Pfaffian numerator estimate]\label{lem:matching}
For every fixed integer $r\ge0$, on a common parameter disk,
\[
 |\partial_u^rG_N(q;u)|
 \le C_r\exp\{-\kappa N^2+C N\log(N+1)\}
\]
uniformly in the real angles and all positive $N$. The constants may
depend on the edge but not on $N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For even $N$, expand only the Schur Pfaffian in the $y_i=e^{\ii q_i}$
variables. Each of its $(N-1)!!$ matchings contains $N/2$ edges. Combine
each matched $y$ factor with its corresponding $\rho$ factor using
\eqref{eq:cancelpair}; bound that complete pair by a constant $C$.
The other $N(N-2)/2$ factors are bounded by $\rho_0$. Thus
\[
 \left|\prod_{i<j}P_{ij}\right|
 \le (N-1)!!\,C^{N/2}\rho_0^{N(N-2)/2}.
\]
For odd $N$, adjoin a ghost variable $-1$ to the $y$ Pfaffian.
Its Schur entry with every real variable is the removable constant one.
There are $N!!$ matchings, with $(N-1)/2$ real matched edges and one
ghost edge, leaving $(N-1)^2/2$ uncanceled $\rho$ factors. This gives
\[
 \left|\prod_{i<j}P_{ij}\right|
 \le N!!\,C^{(N-1)/2}\rho_0^{(N-1)^2/2}.
\]
The identities initially hold away from reciprocal $y$ pairs and extend
by the analytic canceled formula. No division by a vanishing $\rho$
factor occurs. One-body factors, including $B^{N/2}$, cost $C^N$.
These are Gaussian bounds in $N$ up to $\exp(O(N\log(N+1)))$.
Cauchy's inequality on the common disk proves the numerator-jet
statement. It is applied only to $G_N$, not across a pole of
$(1+Z)/(1-Z)$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{All indices in the differentiated tail}
Put $Q_0(q)=\sum_i\dist(q_i,0)^2$. Equation
\eqref{eq:attenuation} implies
\[
 |1-Z|\ge1-|Z|\ge c\min\{1,N\eps+Q_0(q)\}.
\]
All fixed parameter derivatives of $\gamma$ are bounded. Differentiating
the exponential and rational factor consequently gives, for every fixed
$j$ and $0\le r\le j$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:globaljet}
 \left|\partial_u^r\frac{1+Z}{1-Z}\right|
 \le C_j N^j\bigl(1+Q_0(q)^{-j-1}\bigr).
\end{equation}
For $N-1\ge2j+3$, retain just the first $2j+3$ independent angle
squares in $Q_0$. Their inverse $(j+1)$st power is integrable in
$2j+3$ real dimensions, with a constant independent of $N$; all the
unused normalized angular measures have mass one. Lemma~\ref{lem:matching}
therefore implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hightail}
 |\partial_u^j C_N(\ii\eps)|
 \le \frac{C_jN^j}{N!}
       \exp\{-\kappa N^2+C N\log(N+1)\},\qquad N\ge2j+4.
\end{equation}
This sums uniformly in $\eps$.

\subsection{The first amplitude of the complete form factor}
Choose $\phi=2\pi a/p_0$ with $p_0$ an odd prime and
$1\le a\le(p_0-1)/2$. Then the first odd resonance is $n=p_0$ and
the first even resonance is $n=2p_0$. For all lower indices of the
selected parity, the only possible unit-modulus product configuration
has $Z=e^{-\ii N\phi}\ne1$, so those entire form factors are
holomorphic on a neighborhood of the selected point.

\begin{proof}
Subtract the constant and linear terms of $g(t,d_n+v_i)$ in $v_i$.
The linear terms sum to zero, the remaining sum is bounded by $Cq(v)$,
and $\Gamma_{n,t}$ has modulus at least $cn$ on a sufficiently small
common neighborhood.  The quantitative implicit-function theorem gives
the first estimate and a single holomorphic solution on a ball whose
radius is independent of $n$.  Uniqueness gives permutation invariance.
Differentiation along $V_n$ gives
\[
 \nabla_{V_n}T_n
 =-\frac{P\bigl(g_\delta(T_n,d_n+v_i)\bigr)_{i=1}^n}
 {\sum_i g_t(T_n,d_n+v_i)},
 \qquad P=I-\frac1n\mathbf1\mathbf1^T.
\]
The numerator has norm at most $C\norm v_2$ and the denominator has
modulus at least $cn$.  A second differentiation gives the stated
Hessian bound.  All analytic derivative bounds come from the original
fixed bidisk; no dimension-dependent Cauchy radius is used.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The mean correction without division by a quadratic form}

Express $v$ as a function of $w$ and put
\begin{equation}
 \mu_n(w)=\frac1n\sum_iU_i(v(w)).
 \label{eq:morse-mean}
\end{equation}
The common linear coefficient of $U_i$ drops out of this sum.  More
explicitly, at fixed $t$ the expansion has the form
\[
 U_i=a_0(t)v_i+a_1(t)v_i^2+a_2(t,v_i)v_i^3,
 \qquad a_1(t)=O(d_n),
\]
with uniformly bounded analytic coefficients.  Consequently, with
$q=q(w)$,
\begin{align}
 |\mu_n(w)|&\le\frac Cn(|d_n|+\sqrt q)q,\label{eq:morse-mean-bound}\\
 \norm{\nabla\mu_n(w)}_2&\le\frac Cn(|d_n|+\sqrt q)\sqrt q,\label{eq:morse-mean-gradient}\\
 \norm{D^2\mu_n(w)}&\le\frac Cn(|d_n|+\sqrt q).
 \label{eq:morse-mean-hessian}
\end{align}
To obtain these bounds, differentiate the displayed expansion and use
$\sum v_i=0$, the estimates for $T_n$, and the bounded inverse of $G_n$.
Terms from differentiating $T_n$ have an additional factor $1/n$.
The second derivative of $G_n^{-1}$ is bounded by
$C(|d_n|+\norm w_2)$, so composition preserves
\eqref{eq:morse-mean-hessian}.

\begin{proof}
Divide the entire density by its centre value and by $\Delta^2$ before
estimating it.  Every remaining analytic factor is nonzero on a common
small ball, so its logarithm is available there.  The power $n^2/2$
of $B(T_n)$ costs $Cn^2|T_n-\tau_n|$.  For the one-body phases,
\[
 \sum_i|g(T_n,d_n+v_i)-\ii\phi|
 \le C\left(|d_n|\sum_i|v_i|+q(v)+n|T_n-\tau_n|\right).
\]
The sum over all pair-denominator logarithms costs at most $Cn$ times
this last quantity.  The sine divided differences cost
$C\sum_{i<j}|v_i-v_j|^2\le Cnq(v)$.  One-body denominators have the
smaller single-index bound.  Finally, cancellation of the linear term
under $\sum v_i=0$ gives
\[
 \frac{\Gamma_{n,t}(T_n(v),v)}{n g_t(\tau_n,d_n)}
 =1+O(q(v)/n).
\]
Thus the logarithmic cost of the complete residue density is at most
\[
 C\left(n^2|T_n-\tau_n|+n|d_n|\sum_i|v_i|+nq(v)\right)
 \le C\bigl(\sqrt{nq(v)}+nq(v)\bigr).
\]
Combine this estimate with Lemma~\ref{lem:negative-morse}.  No
uncontrolled constant raised to $n^2$ is used in this comparison with
the centre value.
\end{proof}

choose a fixed $c_{\rm pole}>2C_T\sigma$ with

$\Gamma_n$ has only the displayed zero,

$|\Gamma_n|<\pi$.  Thus
$\coth(\Gamma_n/2)-2/\Gamma_n$ is analytic there.  Divide

bound, with polynomial factors in $n$ absorbed into
$\exp(O(n\log(n+1)))$.  Cauchy's estimate on a disk of radius
$c_{\rm pole}/(4n)$ gives~\eqref{eq:morse-boundary-remainder}. This
local subtraction disk is chosen independently of the smaller exterior
disk in Section~\ref{sec:jets}. Reflection
$\delta\mapsto-\delta$ treats the other winding.
\end{proof}

source_context.text:
Here is an explicit tail estimate that also controls the exponential
density bound.  The truncated ball has $x\le Ln$.  For
$\delta\le x\le Ln$ and $j\gg n^2$,
\[
 C\sqrt x+Cx\le\tfrac14j\log(1+x).
\]
If
\[
 Z(\alpha,J)=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}(1+x)^{-J-1}\dd x,
\]
the normalized remaining integral is at most
\begin{equation}
 (1+\delta)^{-j/4}\frac{Z(\alpha_n,j/2)}{Z(\alpha_n,j)}
 \le (1+\delta)^{-j/4}4^{\alpha_n},
 \label{eq:morse-beta-exp-tail}
\end{equation}
provided $\alpha_n\le j/4$.  In the present problem $\alpha_n$ is
an integer, and the last ratio is exactly
\[
 \prod_{r=0}^{\alpha_n-1}\frac{j-r}{j/2-r}\le4^{\alpha_n}.
\]
Thus~\eqref{eq:morse-beta-exp-tail} decreases exponentially in $j$
uniformly when $\alpha_n/j\to0$.  The same estimate without the
exponential density factor bounds the omitted tail of the unperturbed
beta integral.  This proves~\eqref{eq:morse-beta-relative-error}.
\end{proof}

To control the exponential density error outside the small radial region,
use the following beta-tail comparison.  The truncated ball has $x\le Ln$.  For
$\delta\le x\le Ln$ and $j\gg n^2$,
\[
 C\sqrt x+Cx\le\tfrac14j\log(1+x).
\]
If
\[
 Z(\alpha,J)=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}(1+x)^{-J-1}\dd x,
\]
the normalized remaining integral is at most
\begin{equation}
 (1+\delta)^{-j/4}\frac{Z(\alpha_n,j/2)}{Z(\alpha_n,j)}
 \le (1+\delta)^{-j/4}4^{\alpha_n},
 \label{eq:morse-beta-exp-tail}
\end{equation}
provided $\alpha_n\le j/4$.  In the present problem $\alpha_n$ is
an integer, and the last ratio is exactly
\[
 \prod_{r=0}^{\alpha_n-1}\frac{j-r}{j/2-r}\le4^{\alpha_n}.
\]
Thus~\eqref{eq:morse-beta-exp-tail} decreases exponentially in $j$
uniformly when $\alpha_n/j\to0$.  The same estimate without the
exponential density factor bounds the omitted tail of the unperturbed
beta integral.  This proves~\eqref{eq:morse-beta-relative-error}.
\end{proof}

For the inward real approach, \eqref{eq:jets_setting} gives
\[
 \Re\gamma(q;-\eps)\ge
 c\bigl(\eps+\dist(q,\pi)^2\bigr).
\]
Indeed $\Im W=(-\Im B(-\eps))(\eps+1-\cos\delta)$ is positive,
and writing $\gamma=v+\ii\psi$ expresses it as
$\sinh v\sin\psi$, with $\psi$ in a compact subinterval of
$(0,\pi)$. A disk centered at $-\eps$ of radius
$c(\eps+n^{-2})$ consequently preserves the same denominator gap,
up to a fixed factor. Cauchy's estimate there bounds the $j$th
derivative by $j!(Cn^2)^j CnE_n$, uniformly for small $\eps$.
This is summable for every fixed $j$. Differentiation, the boundary
limit, and the particle sum therefore commute by dominated
convergence. This argument proves existence of all boundary jets; it
does not assert a common holomorphic disk for their sum.
\end{proof}

source_context.text:
\subsection{Removing all analytic remainders}

Choose $\sigma>0$ sufficiently small, and then a fixed
$c_{\rm out}>0$ such that
$C_\Gamma c_{\rm out}<c_0\sigma/2$ and
$C_\Gamma(\sigma+c_{\rm out})<\pi/p$.
Here $C_\Gamma$ bounds the phase increments below. On
$|t|<c_{\rm out}/n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_c_over_n_estimate}
 \Re\Gamma_n\ge c_0S-C_\Gamma c_{\rm out},\qquad
 |\Gamma_n-n\ii\phi|\le C_\Gamma(S+c_{\rm out}).
\end{equation}
If $S\ge\sigma$, the first estimate supplies a fixed positive real
part by this choice of $c_{\rm out}$. If $S<\sigma$ and $p\nmid n$, the
second estimate supplies a fixed phase gap: the distance from
$n\phi$ to $2\pi\Z$ is at least $2\pi/p$. Thus the whole
coefficient for $p\nmid n$, and the part with $S\ge\sigma$ for any
$n$, are holomorphic on this $c_{\rm out}/n$ disk with norm at most $CE_n$.
The angular cutoff is fixed and independent of $t$.

\subsection{Removing all analytic remainders}

The local model should be compared only after all terms analytic on
the larger particle-dependent disks have been collected. Their total
Taylor-coefficient growth will be smaller than that of the selected
resonant contribution.

source_context.text:
We also subtract the exact simple parameter pole, not only its
quadratic approximation. In the inner region use the unique small
lifts $q_i=\pi+\delta_i$ and put $v_i=1-\cos\delta_i$. Let
\[
 d_n(t,q)=\frac1nD_n(t,q),\qquad
 a_0=\frac{B(0)}{\sinh(\ii\phi)}\ne0.
\]
On a sufficiently small fixed parameter disk,
\[
 \partial_t d_n(t,q)=a_0+O(|t|+\sigma),
\]
uniformly in $n$ and in $S<\sigma$. Reducing the disk and $\sigma$
makes this derivative lie within $|a_0|/4$ of $a_0$. The quantitative
inverse-function estimate gives a unique zero
$t=T_n(q)=O(S/n)$ and the factorization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_exact_pole_factor}
 D_n(t,q)=n(t-T_n(q))A_n(t,q),\qquad
 A_n(t,q)=\int_0^1\partial_t d_n
       (T_n(q)+u(t-T_n(q)),q)\dd u.
\end{equation}
The factor $A_n$ is analytic and uniformly bounded away from zero on
a smaller fixed disk containing every such $T_n(q)$. The proof can
also be obtained directly by Rouch\'e's theorem on a circle of radius
$CS/n$: $|d_n(0,q)|\le CS/n$, while the derivative differs uniformly
from the nonzero constant $a_0$.

The exact pole is quantitatively close to the average
$\bar v=n^{-1}\sum_i v_i$. At $t=\bar v$, the linear terms in the
analytic expansion of
$\operatorname{arcosh}(b+B(\bar v)(\bar v-v_i))$ sum to zero.
The same uniform inverse-function estimate as above consequently gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_pole_lower}
 T_n(q)=\bar v+O\bigl(\operatorname{Var}(v)\bigr),\qquad
 |T_n(q)|\ge (1-C\sigma)\frac{S(q)}{2n}.
\end{equation}
Here $\operatorname{Var}(v)=n^{-1}\sum_i(v_i-\bar v)^2\le
C\sigma\bar v$, and
$\bar v\ge (1-C\sigma)S/(2n)$. The second estimate concerns the
modulus of a generally complex pole; it does not assert that the
pole is real.

source_context.text:
Write $s=\sin\phi>0$, $\alpha_n=(n^2-1)/2$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_H0}
 H_{0,n}=\frac{|B(0)|^{n^2/2}}
 {n!(2\pi)^{n-1}2^{n(n-1)}s^{n^2}}.
\end{equation}
The complete numerator, evaluated at the pole, satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_numerator_vandermonde}
 |H_n(T_n(q),q)|\le H_{0,n}\Delta(\delta)^2 e^{CnS},
 \qquad \Delta(\delta)=\prod_{i<k}(\delta_i-\delta_k).
\end{equation}
To check the constant and the dependence on $n$, divide every sine
numerator by $(\delta_i-\delta_k)/2$ and every hyperbolic
denominator by $\sinh(\ii\phi)$. Analytic logarithms of the
resulting near-one ratios are bounded by
$C(\delta_i-\delta_k)^2$ and
$C(|T_n|+\delta_i^2+\delta_k^2)$, respectively. Their sums are
$O(nS+n^2|T_n|)=O(nS)$. The one-body factors cost $O(S)$.
Finally the logarithm of
$B(T_n)^{n^2/2}/B(0)^{n^2/2}$ costs $O(n^2|T_n|)$.
This proves \eqref{eq:jets_numerator_vandermonde} with the exact
scale \eqref{eq:jets_H0}, rather than an unspecified constant raised
to the power $n^2$.

\subsection{Completing the all-index comparison}

For $j\to\infty$, split the odd particle indices at
\[
 n_{\mathrm{lo}}=\log j,\qquad
 n_{\mathrm{hi}}=\frac{\sqrt j}{(\log j)^{1/4}}.
\]
The low range, including every nonasymptotic index, is bounded by
Lemma~\ref{lem:jets_boundary_derivatives}:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_low_range}
 \sum_{n\le n_{\mathrm{lo}}}|[t^j]C_n|
 \le\exp\{2j\log\log j+O(j)\}.
\end{equation}
All $c/n$ analytic remainders and the normal-form boundary errors
have the smaller scale
$\exp\{\tfrac12j\log j+O(j)\}$ by
\eqref{eq:jets_remainder_bound} and
\eqref{eq:jets_model_errors}.

\subsection{All ratios and degeneracies in the new argument}
The only ratio excluded from the strict anisotropic-edge mechanism is
$\lambda=1$, where the real-linear determinant degenerates along the
whole isotropic spectral curve. No rationality, algebraicity,
Diophantine bound, or proximity to one is imposed on the other ratios.
For $\lambda\ne1$, the exceptional boundary points consist of the
locally discrete collinear points, corners, elementary zeros or poles
in a chosen chart, and critical points of the edge coordinate. They
are included in the final barrier by density, not declared removable.
Simultaneous imaginary-axis cosine zeros occur exactly for positive
odd-over-odd rational ratios; their local geometry is analyzed in
Section~\ref{sec:geometry} and is likewise included. The near-real-critical
opening of the two spectral edges is nonzero for every unequal positive
ratio, so there is no omitted interval of weak anisotropy.

The following interface is an identity of the actual formulas, rather
than an inference from the labels attached to previous projects. Set
$\lambda=1$ and $s=\sinh z$. Then $S=T=s$, $p=s^2$, $B=1$, and

in \cite{HTsource}, not a diagonal susceptibility or a dual
low-temperature observable.

\newcommand{\XH}{\mathcal X_H}
\newcommand{\XL}{\mathcal X_L}
\newcommand{\norm}[1]{\left\lVert#1\right\rVert}
\title{Natural boundaries of the full bulk susceptibility\newline
for the fixed-ratio anisotropic square-lattice Ising model}
\author{Dehao Lin\\{\small School of Physics, Sun Yat-sen University}\\{\small ORCID: \href{https://orcid.org/0009-0001-4551-8490}{0009-0001-4551-8490}}\\{\small\texttt{lindh9@mail2.sysu.edu.cn}}}
\date{26 October 2026\\{\small Reader edition of the frozen ANISO C001 manuscript}}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For every fixed finite positive coupling ratio, we establish natural
boundaries for the complete bulk magnetic susceptibility on both
physical temperature sides. The high-temperature domain is a bounded
lens; the low-temperature domain is a simply connected epigraph.
We first determine these domains from an independently defined spectral
set and then prove that their full boundaries obstruct continuation.
At regular positive edges, and at either sign of a low-temperature edge,
a nonzero first singular amplitude dominates the entire differentiated
particle tail. Negative high-temperature edges require a different
mechanism: the odd-particle constraint excludes an exact endpoint
resonance, so we use an exact symmetric pole normal form, a
dimension-uniform beta-period estimate, and dominance of one particle
index in selected high Taylor coefficients. The isotropic case follows
from an exact coefficient match to the normalized isotropic results.
The proof retains every lattice site, all particle orders, the physical
field normalization, and the pure-phase low-temperature magnetization
subtraction. Its inputs are the cited real-temperature spin form factors
and the explicitly identified isotropic analytic theorems.
\end{abstract}
\tableofcontents

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Guide to the proof.}
Section~\ref{sec:physical} constructs the complete observable and fixes
the real-physics input. Section~\ref{sec:geometry} identifies its two
spectral domains and the dense regular arcs of their boundaries.
Section~\ref{sec:regular} treats the resonant edges by separating the
first singular term from a uniformly controlled infinite tail.
For negative high-temperature edges, Section~\ref{sec:morse} computes
the local pole contribution and Section~\ref{sec:jets} compares all
particle indices and windings. Section~\ref{sec:closure} then includes
the exceptional points and the isotropic ratio.

The main geometric picture consists of two components of the spectral
complement: a lens around the origin and an epigraph to its right.
The local estimates establish obstructions on dense regular boundary
arcs; the closure argument carries them to every boundary point.

\subsection{Field normalization and state}
Let the magnetic field have energy units, so the finite-volume Hamiltonian
contains $-h\sum_v\sigma_v$, with $\sigma_v\in\{-1,1\}$ and magnetic
moment set to one. Direct differentiation of the finite partition
function gives
\[
 \left.\frac{\partial\langle\sigma_0\rangle}{\partial h}\right|_{h=0}
 =\beta\sum_v\bigl(\langle\sigma_0\sigma_v\rangle
                         -\langle\sigma_0\rangle\langle\sigma_v\rangle\bigr).
\]
Thus the normalized response is the covariance sum $\mathcal X$, and
$\chi=\beta\mathcal X$. A dimensionless field $\eta=\beta h$ instead
has response $\mathcal X$. A specified nonunit magnetic moment multiplies
both by its square.

source_context.text:
The covariance sum also equals the literal uniform-field derivative after
the thermodynamic limit. Here is a precise justification once its finite
absolute sum, proved below, is available. The GHS inequality for arbitrary
nonnegative couplings and site fields \cite[Theorem 1.5]{CGN} says that
truncated two-spin correlations decrease as any nonnegative site field
increases. Pinning the spins removed from a larger plus box by fields
tending to $+\infty$ consequently shows that the plus-box covariances
increase with the box. Their sums converge monotonically to $\mathcal X$.
If $m_V(h)=\langle\sigma_0\rangle_{V,+,h}$, GHS also makes $m_V$
concave for $h\ge0$. Thus
\[
 m_V(h)-m_V(0)\le h m'_V(0)
 =\beta h\sum_{v\in V}\operatorname{Cov}_{V,+,0}(\sigma_0,\sigma_v)
 \le\beta h\mathcal X.
\]
Passing to the plus-state limit gives the upper right-derivative bound
$m'(0+)\le\beta\mathcal X$. Conversely, turn on $h$ only in a finite
set $E$ in the infinite plus state. This is a bounded local change of
measure, so its derivative at zero is exactly
$\beta\sum_{v\in E}\operatorname{Cov}_{+,0}(\sigma_0,\sigma_v)$.
Ferromagnetic field monotonicity makes the uniform-field magnetization
at least this local-field magnetization, with equality at $h=0$.
Letting $E$ increase to the lattice gives the reverse derivative bound.
Hence $m'(0+)=\beta\mathcal X$. In HT, spin-flip symmetry gives the
same derivative from the other side; in LT the stated one-sided
pure-phase convention applies. This argument does not exchange an
uncontrolled magnetic-field limit with an infinite sum.

\section{Exact geometry on every fixed positive coupling slice}\label{sec:geometry}

Fix \(\lambda>0\), and use the one-complex-variable coordinate
\begin{gather*}
 z=2\beta J_x=x+\ii y,\qquad
 a(z)=\sinh z,\quad b(z)=\sinh(\lambda z),\\
 A(z)=\cosh z\cosh(\lambda z),\qquad p(z)=a(z)b(z).
\end{gather*}
The constraint \(K_y=\lambda K_x\) is imposed throughout. In particular,
the ratio \(b/a\) is generally a nonconstant meromorphic function of
\(z\); it must not be identified with the fixed coupling ratio
\(\lambda\).

\section{Regular spectral edges: whole amplitudes and the entire tail}
\label{sec:regular}

At a regular boundary point exactly one of the two real spectral
coordinates is $+1$ or $-1$, the other lies strictly between them, and
the corresponding edge map is a nonramified holomorphic local
coordinate. Interchange the transfer axes when necessary. First take
the endpoint $q_0=0$ and write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positiveedge}
 W(q;u)=b+u+B(u)(1-\cos q),\qquad
 b=\cos\phi,\quad 0<\phi<\pi,\quad \Im B(0)>0.
\end{equation}
Here $u=W(0)-b$ vanishes at the selected point. The opposite sign of
$\Im B$ is obtained by complex conjugation. On the edge, $W(q)$ is
in the upper half-plane except at $q=0$. Its canonical root
$\rho(q)=e^{-\gamma(q)}$ lies in the lower half-disk, with
$\rho(0)=e^{-\ii\phi}$. Compactness gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:halfdisc}
 \Im\rho(q)\le-\delta<0,\qquad |\rho(q)|\le1
 \quad(q\in\R).
\end{equation}
There is no real-angle point with $W=\pm1$. The root, a local
$\gamma$, and all one-body and canceled-pair denominators are therefore
holomorphic on a common fixed complex parameter and angular
neighborhood. On the physical-domain approach $u=\ii\eps$, $\eps>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:attenuation}
 \Re\gamma(q;\ii\eps)\ge c\bigl(\eps+\dist(q,0)^2\bigr).
\end{equation}
Indeed $\Im W=\eps+\Im B(\ii\eps)(1-\cos q)$ is bounded below by
that expression, while
$\Im W=\sinh(\Re\gamma)\sin(\Im\gamma)$ on the compact chosen branch.
The same local side belongs to the physical component bordering the
regular edge, by the geometry of Section~\ref{sec:geometry}.

\begin{lemma}[Matched-Pfaffian numerator estimate]\label{lem:matching}
For every fixed integer $r\ge0$, on a common parameter disk,
\[
 |\partial_u^rG_N(q;u)|
 \le C_r\exp\{-\kappa N^2+C N\log(N+1)\}
\]
uniformly in the real angles and all positive $N$. The constants may
depend on the edge but not on $N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For even $N$, expand only the Schur Pfaffian in the $y_i=e^{\ii q_i}$
variables. Each of its $(N-1)!!$ matchings contains $N/2$ edges. Combine
each matched $y$ factor with its corresponding $\rho$ factor using
\eqref{eq:cancelpair}; bound that complete pair by a constant $C$.
The other $N(N-2)/2$ factors are bounded by $\rho_0$. Thus
\[
 \left|\prod_{i<j}P_{ij}\right|
 \le (N-1)!!\,C^{N/2}\rho_0^{N(N-2)/2}.
\]
For odd $N$, adjoin a ghost variable $-1$ to the $y$ Pfaffian.
Its Schur entry with every real variable is the removable constant one.
There are $N!!$ matchings, with $(N-1)/2$ real matched edges and one
ghost edge, leaving $(N-1)^2/2$ uncanceled $\rho$ factors. This gives
\[
 \left|\prod_{i<j}P_{ij}\right|
 \le N!!\,C^{(N-1)/2}\rho_0^{(N-1)^2/2}.
\]
The identities initially hold away from reciprocal $y$ pairs and extend
by the analytic canceled formula. No division by a vanishing $\rho$
factor occurs. One-body factors, including $B^{N/2}$, cost $C^N$.
These are Gaussian bounds in $N$ up to $\exp(O(N\log(N+1)))$.
Cauchy's inequality on the common disk proves the numerator-jet
statement. It is applied only to $G_N$, not across a pole of
$(1+Z)/(1-Z)$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{All indices in the differentiated tail}
Put $Q_0(q)=\sum_i\dist(q_i,0)^2$. Equation
\eqref{eq:attenuation} implies
\[
 |1-Z|\ge1-|Z|\ge c\min\{1,N\eps+Q_0(q)\}.
\]
All fixed parameter derivatives of $\gamma$ are bounded. Differentiating
the exponential and rational factor consequently gives, for every fixed
$j$ and $0\le r\le j$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:globaljet}
 \left|\partial_u^r\frac{1+Z}{1-Z}\right|
 \le C_j N^j\bigl(1+Q_0(q)^{-j-1}\bigr).
\end{equation}
For $N-1\ge2j+3$, retain just the first $2j+3$ independent angle
squares in $Q_0$. Their inverse $(j+1)$st power is integrable in
$2j+3$ real dimensions, with a constant independent of $N$; all the
unused normalized angular measures have mass one. Lemma~\ref{lem:matching}
therefore implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hightail}
 |\partial_u^j C_N(\ii\eps)|
 \le \frac{C_jN^j}{N!}
       \exp\{-\kappa N^2+C N\log(N+1)\},\qquad N\ge2j+4.
\end{equation}
This sums uniformly in $\eps$.

\[

$k=n^2/2-1$ for even $n$. For every larger same-parity $N$ and

the first estimate and a single holomorphic solution on a ball whose
radius is independent of $n$.  Uniqueness gives permutation invariance.
Differentiation along $V_n$ gives
\[

 =-\frac{P\bigl(g_\delta(T_n,d_n+v_i)\bigr)_{i=1}^n}

\]
The numerator has norm at most $C\norm v_2$ and the denominator has
modulus at least $cn$.  A second differentiation gives the stated
Hessian bound.  All analytic derivative bounds come from the original
fixed bidisk; no dimension-dependent Cauchy radius is used.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The mean correction without division by a quadratic form}

Express $v$ as a function of $w$ and put
\begin{equation}
 \mu_n(w)=\frac1n\sum_iU_i(v(w)).
 \label{eq:morse-mean}
\end{equation}
The common linear coefficient of $U_i$ drops out of this sum.  More
explicitly, at fixed $t$ the expansion has the form
\[
 U_i=a_0(t)v_i+a_1(t)v_i^2+a_2(t,v_i)v_i^3,
 \qquad a_1(t)=O(d_n),
\]
with uniformly bounded analytic coefficients.  Consequently, with
$q=q(w)$,
\begin{align}
 |\mu_n(w)|&\le\frac Cn(|d_n|+\sqrt q)q,\label{eq:morse-mean-bound}\\
 \norm{\nabla\mu_n(w)}_2&\le\frac Cn(|d_n|+\sqrt q)\sqrt q,\label{eq:morse-mean-gradient}\\
 \norm{D^2\mu_n(w)}&\le\frac Cn(|d_n|+\sqrt q).
 \label{eq:morse-mean-hessian}
\end{align}
To obtain these bounds, differentiate the displayed expansion and use
$\sum v_i=0$, the estimates for $T_n$, and the bounded inverse of $G_n$.
Terms from differentiating $T_n$ have an additional factor $1/n$.
The second derivative of $G_n^{-1}$ is bounded by
$C(|d_n|+\norm w_2)$, so composition preserves
\eqref{eq:morse-mean-hessian}.

\begin{proof}
Divide the entire density by its centre value and by $\Delta^2$ before
estimating it.  Every remaining analytic factor is nonzero on a common
small ball, so its logarithm is available there.  The power $n^2/2$
of $B(T_n)$ costs $Cn^2|T_n-\tau_n|$.  For the one-body phases,
\[
 \sum_i|g(T_n,d_n+v_i)-\ii\phi|
 \le C\left(|d_n|\sum_i|v_i|+q(v)+n|T_n-\tau_n|\right).
\]
The sum over all pair-denominator logarithms costs at most $Cn$ times
this last quantity.  The sine divided differences cost
$C\sum_{i<j}|v_i-v_j|^2\le Cnq(v)$.  One-body denominators have the
smaller single-index bound.  Finally, cancellation of the linear term
under $\sum v_i=0$ gives
\[
 \frac{\Gamma_{n,t}(T_n(v),v)}{n g_t(\tau_n,d_n)}
 =1+O(q(v)/n).
\]
Thus the logarithmic cost of the complete residue density is at most
\[
 C\left(n^2|T_n-\tau_n|+n|d_n|\sum_i|v_i|+nq(v)\right)
 \le C\bigl(\sqrt{nq(v)}+nq(v)\bigr).
\]
Combine this estimate with Lemma~\ref{lem:negative-morse}.  No
uncontrolled constant raised to $n^2$ is used in this comparison with
the centre value.
\end{proof}

source_context.text:
Here is an explicit tail estimate that also controls the exponential
density bound.  The truncated ball has $x\le Ln$.  For
$\delta\le x\le Ln$ and $j\gg n^2$,
\[
 C\sqrt x+Cx\le\tfrac14j\log(1+x).
\]
If
\[
 Z(\alpha,J)=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}(1+x)^{-J-1}\dd x,
\]
the normalized remaining integral is at most
\begin{equation}
 (1+\delta)^{-j/4}\frac{Z(\alpha_n,j/2)}{Z(\alpha_n,j)}
 \le (1+\delta)^{-j/4}4^{\alpha_n},
 \label{eq:morse-beta-exp-tail}
\end{equation}
provided $\alpha_n\le j/4$.  In the present problem $\alpha_n$ is
an integer, and the last ratio is exactly
\[
 \prod_{r=0}^{\alpha_n-1}\frac{j-r}{j/2-r}\le4^{\alpha_n}.
\]
Thus~\eqref{eq:morse-beta-exp-tail} decreases exponentially in $j$
uniformly when $\alpha_n/j\to0$.  The same estimate without the
exponential density factor bounds the omitted tail of the unperturbed
beta integral.  This proves~\eqref{eq:morse-beta-relative-error}.
\end{proof}

source_context.text:
\subsection{Removing all analytic remainders}

Choose $\sigma>0$ sufficiently small, and then a fixed
$c_{\rm out}>0$ such that
$C_\Gamma c_{\rm out}<c_0\sigma/2$ and
$C_\Gamma(\sigma+c_{\rm out})<\pi/p$.
Here $C_\Gamma$ bounds the phase increments below. On
$|t|<c_{\rm out}/n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_c_over_n_estimate}
 \Re\Gamma_n\ge c_0S-C_\Gamma c_{\rm out},\qquad
 |\Gamma_n-n\ii\phi|\le C_\Gamma(S+c_{\rm out}).
\end{equation}
If $S\ge\sigma$, the first estimate supplies a fixed positive real
part by this choice of $c_{\rm out}$. If $S<\sigma$ and $p\nmid n$, the
second estimate supplies a fixed phase gap: the distance from
$n\phi$ to $2\pi\Z$ is at least $2\pi/p$. Thus the whole
coefficient for $p\nmid n$, and the part with $S\ge\sigma$ for any
$n$, are holomorphic on this $c_{\rm out}/n$ disk with norm at most $CE_n$.
The angular cutoff is fixed and independent of $t$.

final_context.text:
\subsection{Removing all analytic remainders}

The local model should be compared only after all terms analytic on
the larger particle-dependent disks have been collected. Their total
Taylor-coefficient growth will be smaller than that of the selected
resonant contribution.

source_context.text:
We also subtract the exact simple parameter pole, not only its
quadratic approximation. In the inner region use the unique small
lifts $q_i=\pi+\delta_i$ and put $v_i=1-\cos\delta_i$. Let
\[
 d_n(t,q)=\frac1nD_n(t,q),\qquad
 a_0=\frac{B(0)}{\sinh(\ii\phi)}\ne0.
\]
On a sufficiently small fixed parameter disk,
\[
 \partial_t d_n(t,q)=a_0+O(|t|+\sigma),
\]
uniformly in $n$ and in $S<\sigma$. Reducing the disk and $\sigma$
makes this derivative lie within $|a_0|/4$ of $a_0$. The quantitative
inverse-function estimate gives a unique zero
$t=T_n(q)=O(S/n)$ and the factorization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_exact_pole_factor}
 D_n(t,q)=n(t-T_n(q))A_n(t,q),\qquad
 A_n(t,q)=\int_0^1\partial_t d_n
       (T_n(q)+u(t-T_n(q)),q)\dd u.
\end{equation}
The factor $A_n$ is analytic and uniformly bounded away from zero on
a smaller fixed disk containing every such $T_n(q)$. The proof can
also be obtained directly by Rouch\'e's theorem on a circle of radius
$CS/n$: $|d_n(0,q)|\le CS/n$, while the derivative differs uniformly
from the nonzero constant $a_0$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:jets_discrete_concavity} says that successive
differences of $\ell_k$ decrease by at least $c d^2\log j_n$.
Equation \eqref{eq:jets_selected_j} makes the two adjacent values
equal up to $O_d(1/n)$. It follows first that
$\ell_0-\ell_{\pm1}\ge c'd^2\log j_n$, and then, by summing
the decreasing first differences, that
\[
 \ell_k-\ell_0\le -c''d^2 k^2\log j_n+O_d(|k|/n)
 \qquad(k\ne0).
\]
In particular
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_single_index}
 \sum_{\substack{m\ne n,\ p\mid m,\ m\ \mathrm{odd}\\
                  m\text{ in }\eqref{eq:jets_middle_window}}}
 |M(m,j_n)|
 \le |M(n,j_n)|\,O(j_n^{-c'''d^2}).
\end{equation}
The varying complex phases are immaterial to this modulus
inequality. An $o(1)$ relative error in the local model is
sufficient: the error of the largest index is relative to its own
modulus, while the errors at other indices multiply already
smaller moduli.

\subsection{Completing the all-index comparison}

For $j\to\infty$, split the odd particle indices at
\[
 n_{\mathrm{lo}}=\log j,\qquad
 n_{\mathrm{hi}}=\frac{\sqrt j}{(\log j)^{1/4}}.
\]
The low range, including every nonasymptotic index, is bounded by
Lemma~\ref{lem:jets_boundary_derivatives}:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_low_range}
 \sum_{n\le n_{\mathrm{lo}}}|[t^j]C_n|
 \le\exp\{2j\log\log j+O(j)\}.
\end{equation}
All $c/n$ analytic remainders and the normal-form boundary errors
have the smaller scale
$\exp\{\tfrac12j\log j+O(j)\}$ by
\eqref{eq:jets_remainder_bound} and
\eqref{eq:jets_model_errors}.

In the intermediate range, the error in
\eqref{eq:jets_uniform_model} is uniformly
$O((\log j)^{-1/4})=o(1)$. It remains to compare the higher odd
windings to that model. Let $M_0(n,j)$ be the modulus of
\eqref{eq:jets_model} with $B_n$ replaced by $B(0)$, $h_n$ by
$1$, and $\tau_n$ by $\pi^2/(2n^2)$. The exact formulas give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_baseline_ratio}
 \left|\log\frac{M_0(n,j)}{|M(n,j)|}\right|
 \le C(j/n^2+1)=o(j)
\end{equation}
uniformly in this entire range. Equation
\eqref{eq:jets_winding_bound} is bounded by $CM_0(n,j)$ times
\[
 e^{Cn\sigma}(1-C\sigma)^{-j-1}
 |w|^{-2(j+1-\alpha_n)}.
\]
Here $n=o(j)$ and $\alpha_n/j=o(1)$ uniformly. Choose the fixed
$\sigma$ so small that $-\log(1-C\sigma)<\tfrac12\log3$.
Summing over all odd $|w|\ge3$ then gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jets_higher_windings_negligible}
 \sum_{|w|\ge3}|a_{j,n,w}^{\mathrm{pole}}|
 \le |M(n,j)|e^{-c j}
\end{equation}
for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $j$, uniformly over the
intermediate range. Thus no unexamined winding or particle range
remains between the preceding estimates.

\subsection{All ratios and degeneracies in the new argument}
The only ratio excluded from the strict anisotropic-edge mechanism is
$\lambda=1$, where the real-linear determinant degenerates along the
whole isotropic spectral curve. No rationality, algebraicity,
Diophantine bound, or proximity to one is imposed on the other ratios.
For $\lambda\ne1$, the exceptional boundary points consist of the
locally discrete collinear points, corners, elementary zeros or poles
in a chosen chart, and critical points of the edge coordinate. They
are included in the final barrier by density, not declared removable.
Simultaneous imaginary-axis cosine zeros occur exactly for positive
odd-over-odd rational ratios; their local geometry is analyzed in
Section~\ref{sec:geometry} and is likewise included. The near-real-critical
opening of the two spectral edges is nonzero for every unequal positive
ratio, so there is no omitted interval of weak anisotropy.

\subsection{Exact reuse on the isotropic slice}
The following interface is an identity of the actual formulas, rather
than an inference from the labels attached to previous projects. Set
$\lambda=1$ and $s=\sinh z$. Then $S=T=s$, $p=s^2$, $B=1$, and
\[
 D(x,y;z)=s\left[s+s^{-1}
                  -\tfrac12(x+x^{-1})-\tfrac12(y+y^{-1})\right].
\]
On the positive LT interval $\sqrt p=s$, so every factor
$\sqrt p/D$ in \eqref{eq:doublecorr} is exactly the normalized
isotropic factor in \cite{LTsource}. The even coefficients and the
full-site identity consequently agree term by term, with
$\xi_L=(1-s^{-4})^{1/4}$. In the HT interval the full angular coefficient
in \eqref{eq:fullangular} has $W=s+s^{-1}-\cos q$, and its prefactor
is exactly $(1-s^4)^{1/4}/s$. This is the literal normalized odd sum
in \cite{HTsource}, not a diagonal susceptibility or a dual
low-temperature observable.
In the notation of that HT manuscript its auxiliary exterior variable
is $\widehat t=1/s$; hence our $C_N$ at $s$ is exactly its
$C_N(\widehat t)$, and the reported real condition $\widehat t>1$

\subsection{Exact reuse on the isotropic slice}
The isotropic transfer is an identity of the full coefficient formulas. Set
$\lambda=1$ and $s=\sinh z$. Then $S=T=s$, $p=s^2$, $B=1$, and
\[
 D(x,y;z)=s\left[s+s^{-1}
                  -\tfrac12(x+x^{-1})-\tfrac12(y+y^{-1})\right].
\]
On the positive LT interval $\sqrt p=s$, so every factor
$\sqrt p/D$ in \eqref{eq:doublecorr} is exactly the normalized
isotropic factor in \cite{LTsource}. The even coefficients and the
full-site identity consequently agree term by term, with
$\xi_L=(1-s^{-4})^{1/4}$. In the HT interval the full angular coefficient
in \eqref{eq:fullangular} has $W=s+s^{-1}-\cos q$, and its prefactor
is exactly $(1-s^4)^{1/4}/s$. This is the literal normalized odd sum
in \cite{HTsource}, not a diagonal susceptibility or a dual
low-temperature observable.
In the notation of that HT manuscript its auxiliary exterior variable
is $\widehat t=1/s$; hence our $C_N$ at $s$ is exactly its
$C_N(\widehat t)$, and the reported real condition $\widehat t>1$
is exactly the present physical interval $0<s<1$.

\title{Natural boundaries of the full bulk susceptibility\newline
for the fixed-ratio anisotropic square-lattice Ising model}
\author{Dehao Lin\\{\small School of Physics, Sun Yat-sen University}\\{\small ORCID: \href{https://orcid.org/0009-0001-4551-8490}{0009-0001-4551-8490}}\\{\small\texttt{lindh9@mail2.sysu.edu.cn}}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For every fixed finite positive coupling ratio, we establish natural
boundaries for the complete bulk magnetic susceptibility on both
physical temperature sides. The high-temperature domain is a bounded
lens; the low-temperature domain is a simply connected epigraph.
We first determine these domains from an independently defined spectral
set and then prove that their full boundaries obstruct continuation.
At regular positive edges, and at either sign of a low-temperature edge,
a nonzero first singular amplitude dominates the entire differentiated
particle tail. Negative high-temperature edges require a different
mechanism: the odd-particle constraint excludes an exact endpoint
resonance, so we use an exact symmetric pole normal form, a
dimension-uniform beta-period estimate, and dominance of one particle
index in selected high Taylor coefficients. The isotropic case follows
from an exact coefficient match to the normalized isotropic results.
The proof retains every lattice site, all particle orders, the physical
field normalization, and the pure-phase low-temperature magnetization
subtraction. Its inputs are the cited real-temperature spin form factors
and the explicitly identified isotropic analytic theorems.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Exact reuse on the isotropic slice}
The isotropic transfer is an identity of the full coefficient formulas. Set
$\lambda=1$ and $s=\sinh z$. Then $S=T=s$, $p=s^2$, $B=1$, and
\[
 D(x,y;z)=s\left[s+s^{-1}
                  -\tfrac12(x+x^{-1})-\tfrac12(y+y^{-1})\right].
\]
On the positive LT interval $\sqrt p=s$, so every factor
$\sqrt p/D$ in \eqref{eq:doublecorr} is exactly the normalized
isotropic factor in \cite{LTsource}. The even coefficients and the
full-site identity consequently agree term by term, with
$\xi_L=(1-s^{-4})^{1/4}$. In the HT interval the full angular coefficient
in \eqref{eq:fullangular} has $W=s+s^{-1}-\cos q$, and its prefactor
is exactly $(1-s^4)^{1/4}/s$. This is the literal normalized odd sum
in \cite{HTsource}, not a diagonal susceptibility or a dual
low-temperature observable.
In the notation of that HT manuscript its auxiliary exterior variable
is $\widehat t=1/s$; hence our $C_N$ at $s$ is exactly its
$C_N(\widehat t)$, and the reported real condition $\widehat t>1$
is exactly the present physical interval $0<s<1$.

\title{Natural boundaries of the full bulk susceptibility\newline
for the fixed-ratio anisotropic square-lattice Ising model}
\author{}
\date{}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For every fixed finite positive coupling ratio, we determine natural
boundaries of the complete high-temperature and pure-phase connected
low-temperature bulk susceptibilities. The high-temperature domain is
an explicit bounded lens; the low-temperature domain is an explicit
right epigraph. An endpoint boundary criterion identifies both domains,
and one real-analytic profile difference controls all exceptional
boundary points. On regular positive high-temperature edges and both
low-temperature edge signs, a fixed Vandermonde subproduct gives one
absolute estimate for the entire differentiated particle tail.
At negative high-temperature edges, where odd particles cannot have an
exact endpoint resonance, direct pole expansion on the original real
cycle and an elementary angular concentration estimate give an exact
beta-period model. Selected Taylor orders isolate one particle index
and prove nonextension of the complete odd sum. All lattice sites,
anisotropic factors, physical field normalization and pure-phase
subtraction are retained. At equal coupling a shared constrained-coordinate
proof treats both parities and both high-temperature boundary signs.
Finite-cell contraction, a fixed collision subproduct and an exact
phase-preserving current control the complete differentiated tails.
This proves the equal-coupling boundary internally, including its
hyperbolic-sine covering, without an external natural-boundary theorem.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
For every fixed finite positive coupling ratio, we determine natural
boundaries of the complete high-temperature and pure-phase connected
low-temperature bulk susceptibilities. The high-temperature domain is
an explicit bounded lens; the low-temperature domain is an explicit
right epigraph. An endpoint boundary criterion identifies both domains,

proof treats both parities and both high-temperature boundary signs.
Finite-cell contraction, a fixed collision subproduct and an exact
phase-preserving current control the complete differentiated tails.
The resulting equal-coupling obstruction transfers to the physical
temperature domains through the hyperbolic-sine covering.
\end{abstract}
\section*{Introduction}
The complex-temperature susceptibility of the square-lattice Ising model
is governed by the interaction between singularities of its individual
form-factor integrals and the convergence of their infinite sum.
Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann and Perk \cite[Section 3.2]{ONGP} analyzed the
order dependence of the isotropic singularity amplitudes, while
Boukraa, Hassani and Maillard \cite[Section 6.2]{BHM} studied the
anisotropic cosine-grid singularity equations and their accumulation
in two complex couplings. Fixing the positive physical coupling ratio
selects a one-complex-variable temperature slice and its two physical
continuations.

\section*{Introduction}
The complex-temperature susceptibility of the square-lattice Ising model
is governed by the interaction between singularities of its individual

We prove natural boundaries for the full bulk susceptibilities on
the explicit fixed-ratio domains stated below. The proof uses endpoint
profiles to determine the domains, a retained Vandermonde subproduct
to control all higher particle orders at regular edges, and a direct
comparison of pole integrals on the real cycle at negative
high-temperature edges. Section~\ref{sec:iso-internal} proves the
equal-coupling case by a unified contour deformation and

and complete lattice sum. Section~\ref{sec:geometry} determines the
spectral domains and the dense regular arcs. Sections~\ref{sec:regular}
and \ref{sec:realcycle}--\ref{sec:jets} prove the two local
noncancellation mechanisms, and Section~\ref{sec:closure} includes the
exceptional anisotropic boundary points. Section~\ref{sec:iso-internal}
then supplies the isotropic estimates and the temperature covering.

boundaries of the complete high-temperature and pure-phase connected
low-temperature bulk susceptibilities. The high-temperature domain is
an explicit bounded lens; the low-temperature domain is an explicit
right epigraph. An endpoint boundary criterion identifies both domains,
and one real-analytic profile difference controls all exceptional
boundary points. On regular positive high-temperature edges and both
low-temperature edge signs, a fixed Vandermonde subproduct gives one
absolute estimate for the entire differentiated particle tail.
At negative high-temperature edges, where odd particles cannot have an
exact endpoint resonance, direct pole expansion on the original real
cycle and an elementary angular concentration estimate give an exact
beta-period model. Selected Taylor orders isolate one particle index
and prove nonextension of the complete odd sum. All lattice sites,
anisotropic factors, physical field normalization and pure-phase
subtraction are retained. At equal coupling a shared constrained-coordinate
proof treats both parities and both high-temperature boundary signs.
Finite-cell contraction, a fixed collision subproduct and an exact
phase-preserving current control the complete differentiated tails.
The resulting equal-coupling obstruction transfers to the physical
temperature domains through the hyperbolic-sine covering.
\end{abstract}
\section*{Introduction}
The complex-temperature susceptibility of the square-lattice Ising model
is governed by the interaction between singularities of its individual
form-factor integrals and the convergence of their infinite sum.
Orrick, Nickel, Guttmann and Perk \cite[Section 3.2]{ONGP} analyzed the
order dependence of the isotropic singularity amplitudes, while
Boukraa, Hassani and Maillard \cite[Section 6.2]{BHM} studied the
anisotropic cosine-grid singularity equations and their accumulation
in two complex couplings. Fixing the positive physical coupling ratio
selects a one-complex-variable temperature slice and its two physical
continuations.

We prove natural boundaries for the full bulk susceptibilities on
the explicit fixed-ratio domains stated below. The proof uses endpoint
profiles to determine the domains, a retained Vandermonde subproduct
to control all higher particle orders at regular edges, and a direct
comparison of pole integrals on the real cycle at negative
high-temperature edges. Section~\ref{sec:iso-internal} proves the
equal-coupling case by a unified contour deformation and
phase-preserving current argument for both particle parities.

Section~\ref{sec:physical} fixes the physical state, field normalization
and complete lattice sum. Section~\ref{sec:geometry} determines the
spectral domains and the dense regular arcs. Sections~\ref{sec:regular}
and \ref{sec:realcycle}--\ref{sec:jets} prove the two local
noncancellation mechanisms, and Section~\ref{sec:closure} includes the
exceptional anisotropic boundary points. Section~\ref{sec:iso-internal}
then supplies the isotropic estimates and the temperature covering.

source_context.text:
We next check that every remaining physical boundary point has all
the regularity properties used by the particle estimates, without
separately classifying collinear candidates.
Write $D=\Im(\overline S T)$.
Suppose $x>0$, $F_1=0$ and $F_2\ne0$.  By the endpoint criterion,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpointrepresentation}
 A=Su+\epsilon T,\qquad
 u\in[-1,1],\qquad \epsilon=\operatorname{sign}(\cos y).
\end{equation}
The following identity is decisive:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-defect}
 D^2(1-u^2)=\tanh^2(\lambda x)F_2(x,y)^2.
\end{equation}
Here is a short derivation including the endpoint cases.
Put $K=\cosh z\,T-\epsilon\cosh(\lambda z)$.
Direct expansion gives $K^2=S^2(u^2-1)$, so
\[
 \bigl[\Re(\overline K T)\bigr]^2=D^2(1-u^2).
\]
Writing $c=\cosh x$, $h=\sinh x$,
$C=\cosh(\lambda x)$, $H=\sinh(\lambda x)$,
the relation $F_1=0$ is $\cos y=\epsilon cH/C$, and hence
\begin{align*}
 \Re(\overline K T)
 &=c\cos y\,|T|^2-\epsilon HC\\
 &=\epsilon\frac HC\left(c^2(C^2-\cos^2(\lambda y))-C^2\right)
 =-\epsilon\frac HC F_2.
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{eq:endpoint-defect}.  Its right side is positive,
so $D\ne0$ and $u\in(-1,1)$.

Direct differentiation at the center gives
\[
 g(\tau_n,d_n)=\ii\phi,\qquad
 g_t(\tau_n,d_n)=-\frac{\ii B_n}{s},\qquad
 \frac12g_{\delta\delta}(\tau_n,d_n)=\frac{\ii B_nh_n}{2s}.
\]
Evenness in $\delta$ gives $g_{\delta\delta\delta}(t,d_n)=O(d_n)$.
Writing $u=T_n-\tau_n$, Taylor expansion of
\eqref{eq:rc-pole-equation}, with the linear terms canceled by
$\sum v_i=0$, therefore gives on the real ball
\[
 0=ng_t(\tau_n,d_n)u+\tfrac12g_{\delta\delta}(\tau_n,d_n)Q
 +O\left(n|u|^2+|u|Q+d_n\sum_i|v_i|^3+\sum_i v_i^4\right).
\]
Using \eqref{eq:rc-pole-coarse}, we obtain the following estimate:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rc-pole-error}
 \begin{split}
 T_n(v)&=T_{0,n}(v)+\mathcal R_n(v),\qquad
 T_{0,n}(v)=\tau_n+\frac{h_nQ}{2n},\\
 |\mathcal R_n(v)|&\le\frac Cn\left(
       \frac1n\sum_i|v_i|^3+\sum_i v_i^4+\frac{Q^2}{n}\right).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
In particular, since $\sum|v_i|^3\le Q^{3/2}$ and
$\sum v_i^4\le Q^2$, a sufficiently small fixed $\sigma$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rc-small-error}
 |\mathcal R_n(v)|\le\tfrac14D_n(v),\qquad
 D_n(v):=\tau_n+\frac{a_nQ}{2n}\le |T_{0,n}(v)|
 \quad(Q<\sigma).
\end{equation}
No nonlinear change of variables is required.

All constants in \eqref{eq:jets_model} can be checked directly.
At the collision $\gamma_i=\ii\phi$, the numerator divided by
$\Delta^2$ is
\[
 -\frac{\ii B_n^{n^2/2}}
       {n!(2\pi)^{n-1}2^{n(n-1)}s^{n^2}},
 \qquad \Gamma_t=-\frac{\ii nB_n}s.
\]
Multiplication by $-2/\Gamma_t$, followed by the exact complex quadratic beta integral, gives half of \eqref{eq:jets_model}.
Reflection $\delta\mapsto-\delta$ preserves the full integrand and
exchanges the first two winding sectors, giving the displayed
factor of two. The factor $B_n^{\alpha_n-1/2}$ retains its quadratic
particle-dependent phase. No positivity across particle indices is
being assumed.

\subsection{Exact coefficient interface on the isotropic slice}
Set $\lambda=1$ and $s=\sinh z$. Then $S=T=s$, $p=s^2$, $B=1$, and
\[
 D(x,y;z)=s\left[s+s^{-1}
                  -\tfrac12(x+x^{-1})-\tfrac12(y+y^{-1})\right].
\]
On the positive LT interval $\sqrt p=s$, so every factor
$\sqrt p/D$ in \eqref{eq:doublecorr} is exactly the normalized
isotropic factor in \cite[Section 2 and Appendix F]{LTsource}.
The even coefficients and the full-site identity agree term by term.
In particular the function to which the isotropic result applies is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iso-LT-interface}
 \mathcal X_L(s)=M^2\sum_{N\ge2,\ N\ {\rm even}}C_N(s)
 =1-M^2+2M^2\sum_{N\ge2,\ N\ {\rm even}}T_N(s),
 \qquad M^2=(1-s^{-4})^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
The onsite term $1-M^2$ follows from the complete connected correlation
sum; no lattice site is omitted.

$\sqrt N(2\pi)^{N-1}$.  For $N=1$ the constrained integral is evaluation
at its single angle.  All pair factors are rational squares, so no
choice of half-angle or logarithm changes the coefficient.  Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iso-exterior-coefficients}
 C_N^\sigma(t)=\mathcal F_N^\sigma(t+t^{-1}),\qquad |t|>1.
\end{equation}
The compact normal-convergence bounds for the full product apply to
each fixed differentiated series here.  To see directly that the
auxiliary sign causes no change, on a compact dispersion neighborhood
all roots satisfy $|\rho_i|\le q<1$ and have imaginary parts of one
sign.  The latter fact follows from
$\Im W_i=\Im\rho_i(1-|\rho_i|^{-2})/2$.
The identity
\[
 |1-vw|^2-|v-w|^2
   =(1-|v|^2)(1-|w|^2)+4\Im v\Im w
\]
therefore bounds every root Schur factor
$|(\rho_i-\rho_j)/(1-\rho_i\rho_j)|$ strictly below one, uniformly.
Expand the angular Schur product by the matching identity proved
in Section~\ref{sec:physical} and cancel each matched angular pole
with its corresponding root factor.  The resulting complete matched
pairs are bounded; all but $O(N)$ root factors retain the strict
contraction.  The number of matchings costs
$\exp(O(N\log(N+1)))$, while the unmatched root factors supply
$\exp(-cN^2)$.  This gives a summable coefficient bound on the
normalized constrained torus for either sign.  All one-body factors
and $1-\sigma Z$ have fixed gaps there.  Cauchy's inequality on a
slightly larger compact neighborhood gives every fixed derivative.
No determinant representation is needed in this specialization.

Set $b=\arccos(\mathsf S_*-1)$; then $\alpha<b<2\alpha$.
Choose a smooth periodic $p$, supported in $(0,\pi)$, with
$0\le p\le1$ and $p=1$ on $[\delta,\pi-\delta]$; put
$m(\theta)=p(-\theta)$.  The endpoint width $\delta$ is small,
so both $\pm b$ lie in the corresponding plateaus.  With a small
fixed $\tau>0$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iso-balanced-deformation}
 P=\sum_i p(\theta_i),\quad Q=\sum_i m(\theta_i),\quad
 h_i=\frac\tau N(Pm(\theta_i)-Qp(\theta_i)),\quad
 y_i(\xi)=e^{i\theta_i+\xi h_i},\quad 0\le\xi\le1.
\end{equation}
The sum of the $h_i$ is zero, so the constrained product of the $y_i$
is unchanged.  For $y=e^{h+i\theta}$,
\[
 \Im\left(\mathsf S-\frac{y+y^{-1}}2\right)
       =\Im\mathsf S-\sinh h\sin\theta.
\]
The motion is inward on the upper semicircle and outward on the lower
one.  Its imaginary part therefore remains positive throughout the
homotopy.  All roots stay on the interior sheet, all one-body and pair
denominators stay nonzero, and $|Z|<1$.  The complete holomorphic
integrand can consequently be transported over this closed constrained
torus.  No partition is imposed before the homotopy.

Use the filled analytic divided differences
\[
 \mathcal U_{il}=\int_0^1U_v(v_l+t(v_i-v_l))\,dt,\qquad
 \mathcal E_{il}=\int_0^1U_{vv}(v_l+t(v_i-v_l))\,dt.
\]
The convex inverse domain gives $\Re\mathcal E_{il}\ge c$.
Define the analytic field
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iso-covariance-field}
 \begin{gathered}
 D_U=\sum_{i<l}(U_i-U_l)^2,\qquad
 H_{il}=\frac{(v_i-v_l)\mathcal U_{il}^2}{\mathcal E_{il}},
 \qquad G_i=\sum_lH_{il},\\
 A=-\sum_iU_{\mathsf S,i},\qquad B_i=AG_i/D_U.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
There is no pair pole: $H_{il}$ is analytic also at $v_i=v_l$.
Away from equality it equals $(U_i-U_l)^2/(U_{v,i}-U_{v,l})$.
Antisymmetry and pairing give
\[
 \sum_iG_i=0,\qquad \sum_iU_{v,i}G_i=D_U,\qquad
 \sum_iB_i=0,\qquad \sum_iU_{v,i}B_i=-\sum_iU_{\mathsf S,i}.
\]
Thus the field has both exact transport identities.

Combining \eqref{eq:iso-transported-density} with
Lemma~\ref{lem:iso-coarea} bounds a right shell at a fixed mean by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iso-one-shell}
 \frac{C_jN^{C_j}}{N!}e^{-\kappa N^2+C_jN}
 \Delta^{D_\ell+N-3-2j}(1+|\log\eps|).
\end{equation}
Its exponent is positive for every $N\ge n_*+2$ and $j\le k$:
it is at least $n_*+N-2$ in the odd case and $n_*+N-1$ in the
even case.  For fixed $\mu,\eps$,
\[
 \frac{\Delta(r_0/2)}{\Delta(r_0)}
 =\frac12\sqrt{\frac{|\mu|+r_0+\eps}{|\mu|+r_0/2+\eps}}
       \in[1/2,1/\sqrt2].
\]
The dyadic sum is therefore bounded uniformly in the mean by a geometric series.
Its largest possible scale is fixed; its power costs only $C^N$
times a fixed constant.  This is absorbed into the linear exponential
in \eqref{eq:iso-one-shell}.  Summing the at most $CN$ means adds
only a polynomial factor.  No small/large-scale division or finite
intermediate particle range is required.  The mixed, anchored, and
right pieces consequently obey, for all higher orders,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iso-every-order-tail}
 |\partial_{\mathsf S}^j\mathcal F_N^\sigma(\mathsf S_\eps)|
 \le C_j(1+|\log\eps|)
 \left(C_j^NN^{-N/2+C_j}
       +\frac{N^{C_j}}{N!}e^{-\kappa N^2+C_jN}\right).
\end{equation}
Both envelopes are summable.  The exact split
\eqref{eq:iso-exact-split} proves Theorem~\ref{thm:iso-tail}.
The parameter-change assertion follows from the finite chain rule.
